issues.legal_issue: A long and uninterrupted practice of encashing privilege leave for established purposes may become a condition of service, and its unjustified withdrawal is impermissible.
material_facts: The employer had repeatedly permitted workers to encash privilege leave for specified purposes over a long period.
The Tribunal found the practice to have continued without interruption and to have become a condition of service.
The employer refused some applications after the practice had been followed for years; the evidence supported the Tribunal’s finding of the practice.
issues.conclusion: The Court upheld the Tribunal’s finding that the encashment practice had ripened into a condition of service and that the employer’s departure from it was without lawful reason.
issues.legal_principle: A long and continued practice, established on the evidence, may ripen into a condition of service. The Court found no basis to interfere with the Tribunal’s factual finding. No statutory provision or earlier case was relied on for this issue.

rule.if: appeal_from_industrial_award and repeated_encashment_requests_were_granted and the_practice_was_long_and_uninterrupted and management_later_refused_requests

predicates.appeal_from_industrial_award: An appeal is brought against an industrial award concerning employees’ service conditions.
predicates.repeated_encashment_requests_were_grante: The employer repeatedly granted employees’ requests to encash leave.
predicates.the_practice_was_long_and_uninterrupted: The encashments formed a long-running, uninterrupted practice for established purposes.
predicates.management_later_refused_requests: The employer later refused requests that fell within the established practice.

issues.definition: When an appeal from an industrial award concerns a long, uninterrupted practice of granting leave-encashment requests and the employer later refuses such requests, the practice is treated as a condition of service.

issues.legal_issue: Subordinate staff may be granted more privilege leave than the statutory minimum where the industrial tribunal finds their lesser entitlement unjustified compared with that of clerical staff.
material_facts: Clerical staff received 30 days of privilege leave annually, while subordinate staff received 15 days.
The Tribunal found the difference in privilege leave unjustified and awarded subordinate staff the same privilege leave as clerical staff.
The applicable legislation prescribed a minimum of 15 days of privilege leave.
issues.conclusion: The Court upheld the Tribunal’s direction granting subordinate staff 30 days of privilege leave, holding that the statutory minimum did not prevent a greater entitlement.
issues.legal_principle: Section 22(1)(a) of the Delhi Shops and Establishments Act, 1954 prescribed a minimum of 15 days of privilege leave. That minimum did not prevent the Tribunal from awarding 30 days. No earlier case was relied on for this issue.

predicates.appeal_from_industrial_award: An appeal is brought against an industrial award concerning employees’ service conditions.
predicates.subordinate_staff_received_less_privileg: Subordinate staff received less annual privilege leave than clerical staff.
predicates.the_statutory_privilege_leave_requiremen: The applicable leave requirement set a minimum entitlement rather than a maximum.
predicates.the_difference_was_found_unjustified: The Tribunal found no justification for the difference in privilege leave between the employee groups.

issues.definition: Where subordinate staff receive less privilege leave than clerical staff, the applicable requirement is only a minimum, and the difference is found unjustified, a greater privilege-leave entitlement may be upheld.

issues.legal_issue: An industrial tribunal cannot award sickness and casual leave beyond a mandatory statutory ceiling for those forms of leave combined.
material_facts: The Tribunal directed that subordinate staff receive sickness and casual leave on the same basis as clerical staff.
The combined sickness and casual leave awarded exceeded the statutory maximum of 12 days per year.
Section 22(1)(b) of the Delhi Shops and Establishments Act, 1954 fixed a maximum total period of 12 days for sickness or casual leave with wages.
The clerical staff’s receipt of leave beyond that maximum did not, in the Court’s view, authorize the Tribunal to disregard the statutory limit.
issues.conclusion: The Court set aside the award to the extent that it directed sickness and casual leave exceeding a total of 12 days in a year.
issues.legal_principle: Section 22(1)(b) of the Delhi Shops and Establishments Act, 1954 imposed a maximum total entitlement to paid sickness or casual leave. A tribunal cannot disregard that mandatory limit, even if another employee group receives more. No earlier case was relied on for this issue.

predicates.appeal_from_industrial_award: An appeal is brought against an industrial award concerning employees’ service conditions.
predicates.the_applicable_rule_sets_a_mandatory_com: The applicable rule fixes a mandatory maximum for paid sickness and casual leave combined.
predicates.the_tribunal_awarded_sick_and_casual_lea: The Tribunal’s award grants paid sickness and casual leave in excess of the combined maximum.

issues.definition: When an appeal concerns an award that exceeds a mandatory combined ceiling on paid sickness and casual leave, the excess award must be set aside.
